Start with three things: **confirm your right to live and work there, set a realistic budget, and arrange somewhere to stay when you arrive.** Those decisions shape the rest of the move.

### Before you leave
- **Check immigration rules on official government websites.** Confirm visa processing times, whether you can work on arrival, what permits family members need, and whether you must register after entering. Avoid nonrefundable bookings until your visa is approved.
- **Gather documents while they’re easy to get.** Check passport validity and collect birth or marriage certificates, medical and vaccination records, prescriptions, and school or professional records. Check which documents need certified translations or authentication, and keep secure copies you can access abroad.
- **Budget for setup costs, not just the flight.** Include temporary housing, a rental deposit, shipping, health coverage, and a cushion in case your first paycheck or permanent housing takes longer than expected. Check how the move may affect your taxes and keep a backup way to access money.
- **Plan for the first few weeks.** Book temporary housing if you can, so you can see neighborhoods and rentals in person before committing. Confirm when health coverage starts and check whether your medications can legally be brought into the country. If you’re bringing children or pets, check school enrollment and pet import rules early.

### After you arrive
Handle anything with a deadline first: address registration, residence permits, and tax or social insurance IDs, as applicable. Then set up a phone, banking, and healthcare. Keep your passport, entry documents, essential medication, and first-night address in your carry-on rather than in shipped luggage.

If you share **where you’re moving from and to, your target date, and whether it’s for work, study, or family**, I can turn this into a country-specific timeline.

Start by checking the destination country’s official immigration website. Confirm what visa or residence permit you need, whether it lets you work, and what you’ll need to do after arrival. Gather documents such as your passport, birth certificate, medical records, and proof of employment or savings. Check whether any need certified translations or authentication before you leave, when they’re often easier to arrange.

Make a budget for the first few months, including temporary housing, a rental deposit, transport, health insurance, and a cushion in case your first paycheck is delayed. If you don’t know the area, book a short stay rather than committing to a long lease from abroad. Before you go, make sure you can access your money and receive bank verification codes overseas, and check how you’ll refill any regular prescriptions.

Plan your first week before you leave. Know how you’ll get from the airport or station to your accommodation, which appointments or registrations have deadlines, and how you’ll get a local phone number. Save your address, key documents, and emergency contacts somewhere you can reach offline. Once the essentials are handled, give yourself time to settle in. A language class, a hobby group, or even a regular visit to the same café can help a new place start to feel familiar.

Your goal in week one isn’t to prove you know everything. It’s to learn what matters, meet the people you’ll work with, and agree on what to tackle first.

- **Ask your manager what success looks like.** Try: “What would make this a good first week? What should I be able to do on my own by the end of the month?”
- **Get to know your immediate teammates.** Ask what they work on, where your roles overlap, and how they prefer to handle quick questions.
- **Keep a running set of notes.** Record names, acronyms, useful links, and open questions. Group nonurgent questions for a check-in, but speak up right away if you’re blocked.
- **Learn how the team works.** Notice where decisions get made, what belongs in chat versus email, and when people expect updates. If a process seems odd, ask why it exists before suggesting a change.
- **Aim for one small, useful contribution.** Ask your manager or a teammate for a task that helps the team while teaching you how the work gets done.
- **Close the week with a quick recap.** Tell your manager what you learned, flag anything still blocking you, and confirm your top priority for next week.

If you forget a name or need to ask a question twice, don’t sweat it. Being curious and following through matters more than looking like you’ve already settled in.

In your first few days, focus on learning how the team works rather than trying to prove yourself. Ask your manager what a good first week looks like, what to prioritize, and how they prefer to get updates. Keep a running note of names, acronyms, and questions so you can look things up later or bring a few questions to your next check-in.

Make an effort to meet the people you’ll work with most. A simple “What are you working on, and where might our work overlap?” can tell you more than a formal introduction. Pay attention to which conversations happen in chat, which need a meeting, and where decisions are written down.

If you have room, look for one small, useful task you can finish by Friday. It’s a low-pressure way to learn the workflow and get feedback. At the end of the week, check in with your manager about what you’ve learned, anything you’re blocked on, and what to tackle next. You don’t need to have it all figured out; knowing who to ask and what to do next is a good start.

Start with a **consistent wake-up time**, even after a rough night. Get some outdoor light soon after you wake, and give yourself enough time to sleep—most adults need 7–9 hours.

A few other changes worth trying:

- **Stop caffeine at least 6 hours before bed.** If you’re sensitive to it, try making lunch your cutoff.
- **Give yourself a wind-down period.** Dim the lights and spend the last 30–60 minutes doing something calm. Keep your bedroom cool, dark, and quiet.
- **Go to bed when you’re sleepy.** If you’re lying awake and getting frustrated, get up and do something quiet in dim light. Return when you feel sleepy, rather than watching the clock.
- **Avoid using alcohol as a sleep aid.** It can make you drowsy at first but disrupt sleep later in the night.

If sleep trouble persists or affects your daytime functioning, talk with a healthcare professional. **Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I)** is a first-line treatment for chronic insomnia. Loud snoring, gasping during sleep, or significant daytime sleepiness are also worth getting checked.

Is your main issue falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up tired even after enough hours?

Start by getting up at about the same time every day, even after a rough night. Get some daylight soon after waking, and give yourself enough time for sleep—most adults need seven to nine hours. Go to bed when you feel sleepy rather than trying to force an early bedtime.

Make the last hour before bed quieter. Dim the lights, put aside work or anything that gets you keyed up, and keep your room cool, dark, and quiet. If you drink caffeine, try stopping at least six hours before bedtime, or earlier if you’re sensitive to it. Alcohol can make you feel sleepy at first but disrupt sleep later in the night.

If you’re lying awake and getting frustrated, get out of bed and do something quiet in dim light, then return when you feel sleepy. Try not to watch the clock. If sleep problems persist or affect how you function during the day, talk with a healthcare professional. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia is a first-line treatment for ongoing insomnia, and loud snoring, gasping during sleep, or marked daytime sleepiness are reasons to ask about sleep apnea.

Before adopting a dog, ask yourself: **Can I meet this dog’s needs on an ordinary workday, not just on a good weekend?** The right match matters more than breed or appearance.

- **Time and routine.** Dogs need daily exercise, bathroom breaks, companionship, and training. Puppies need especially frequent supervision and potty breaks. If you work long shifts or travel often, make a realistic plan for a walker, sitter, or other help.
- **Budget.** The adoption fee is just the start. Price out food, routine vet care, parasite prevention, and any grooming, training, or boarding you’ll need. Plan for emergency vet bills with savings, insurance, or both.
- **Housing and household.** Confirm your lease rules and any pet fees or restrictions. Make sure everyone in the home agrees on who does what. If you have children or other pets, ask how the dog has behaved around them and how to manage introductions.
- **The dog’s individual needs.** Ask the shelter or foster what they’ve actually observed: How does the dog handle being alone, walking on leash, or meeting other animals? Ask about medical needs, any bite history or guarding around food and toys, and what’s still unknown. An adult dog with a known foster history may be a more predictable fit than a puppy.
- **The first few weeks.** Set up a quiet resting spot, keep the routine predictable, and introduce visitors and other pets gradually. Arrange a vet visit, confirm the microchip registration, and use reward-based training. Don’t judge the fit solely by the first day; behavior can change as a dog settles in.

If you’re unsure, ask whether the rescue offers **foster-to-adopt** and what support it provides after adoption. Before you commit, make a concrete plan for a typical weekday, your next trip, and an unexpected vet bill.

Think about what life with a dog would look like on your busiest day, not just your best day. Dogs need daily exercise, bathroom breaks, companionship, and training. A puppy usually needs more supervision and more frequent trips outside, while an adult dog may have a more established routine. Check your housing rules and think about who will care for the dog when you work late, travel, or get sick.

Budget beyond the adoption fee. Food, supplies, routine vet visits, and parasite prevention add up, and you may also need to pay for grooming, training, or boarding. Have a plan for unexpected vet bills, whether that’s savings or pet insurance. Make sure everyone in your household agrees on the adoption and knows who will handle the daily care.

Choose a dog whose needs fit your household rather than going by looks or breed alone. Ask the shelter or foster carer what they’ve observed about the dog’s energy level, medical history, and behavior around children, other pets, and when left alone. They may not know everything, so meet the dog and ask whether a trial or foster-to-adopt period is available if you’re unsure.

Once you bring the dog home, keep the first few days quiet and predictable. Give them a safe place to rest, start a simple routine, and schedule a vet visit to review their records and care needs. Some dogs settle in quickly and others take weeks or longer, so don’t judge the fit by the first day alone.

Start with a small buffer, not a big savings goal. If you’re living paycheck to paycheck, even $25 set aside can help you avoid an overdraft or cover a small surprise.

1. **Plan from payday to payday.** On payday, write down your balance and what you’ll need before the next check: rent and bills due, groceries, transportation, and minimum debt payments. This tells you what you can safely set aside.
2. **Save a small amount only if it fits.** If there’s $5 left after essentials, move it to a separate, no-fee savings account or a savings bucket in your banking app. Start manually if your income varies; an automatic transfer isn’t worth an overdraft fee.
3. **If there’s nothing left, don’t force it.** If bills come due before your paycheck, ask whether you can change a due date. If essentials consistently cost more than you bring in, focus first on closing that gap: check for utility or grocery assistance, ask about hardship plans, or review recurring bills for a cost you can cut without creating a bigger problem.
4. **Build in steps.** Try $25, then $100, then enough to cover a week of essentials. If you use the money for an unexpected expense, it did its job. Start rebuilding when you can.

A good first move today: list everything that needs to be paid before your next payday. That will help you see whether your next step is saving a few dollars or freeing up room first.

Start by looking at what has to be paid before your next paycheck, rather than trying to build a whole monthly budget at once. Set aside enough for essentials like rent, food, utilities, and getting to work. If there’s a little left, move an amount you’re confident you won’t need back—even $5—into a separate, no-fee savings account. Skip the transfer if it might cause an overdraft or leave you short on a bill.

Make your first goal small enough to reach. A $50 cushion won’t cover every emergency, but it could keep a surprise expense from turning into a late fee or another charge on your credit card. If you need to spend the money on an actual surprise, that’s what it’s there for. Start building it back up when you can.

If there’s consistently nothing left, don’t force yourself to save. Look for one change that could give you some breathing room: ask whether a bill’s due date can move closer to payday, check whether you qualify for grocery or utility assistance, or see if a recurring bill can be lowered. The first win may be getting through a pay period without falling further behind.

A good work-from-home routine makes it clear **what to work on, when you’re available, and when you’re done**.

- **Pick one must-finish task.** Before opening email or chat, write down a concrete result for the day: “Send the first draft,” not “Work on the proposal.”
- **Protect one focus block.** Put 45–90 minutes on your calendar during your best-energy window. Silence nonurgent notifications and keep your phone out of reach. If your job is interruption-heavy, start with 25 minutes.
- **Set expectations about replies.** If your role allows it, check messages between focus blocks instead of continuously. Let teammates know how to reach you when something is genuinely urgent.
- **Take breaks away from your desk.** A short walk or lunch in another room gives you a real break rather than just a different screen.
- **End with a five-minute shutdown.** Note where you stopped, write down tomorrow’s first step, and close your work apps. You don’t need a separate office for this to work.

Start with just the first two for a week. Judge the experiment by whether you finished more of the work that mattered, not whether you spent more time at your desk.

Start each day by deciding what would make it feel productive. Pick one task that matters most and give it a block of time on your calendar. If you can, do it before opening email or chat. If you need to be reachable, let coworkers know when you’ll be heads-down and how to reach you for anything urgent.

Make it easier to focus than to get distracted. Put your phone out of reach, close tabs you don’t need, and keep a scrap of paper nearby for chores or ideas that pop into your head. When you take a break, step away from the screen. A short walk or lunch away from your desk can help you come back with more energy than checking another app.

Give the workday a clear ending. Take five minutes to note what you finished and write down the first thing you’ll do tomorrow. Then close your laptop or put your work materials away. If a routine isn’t working, change one thing at a time and judge it by whether you’re finishing meaningful work, not by how many hours you spend at your desk.

Start with the behavior you want to change, not the coworker’s personality. “They keep interrupting me in meetings” gives you something concrete to address; “they’re difficult” doesn’t.

- **Address it privately if it feels safe.** Name what happened, explain the impact, and make a specific request: “In today’s meeting, I didn’t get to finish explaining the timeline. Next time, can you let me finish before we discuss concerns?” Give them a chance to share their perspective, too.
- **Set a boundary in the moment.** A calm “I’d like to finish my point, then I’m happy to hear yours” can be more useful than waiting for a bigger conversation. If the issue is missed handoffs or changing expectations, confirm who owns what and by when in writing.
- **Escalate a pattern, not a personality clash.** If the problem continues, bring a few factual examples to your manager, explain how it affects the work, and ask for a specific change. If it involves harassment, discrimination, threats, or retaliation, you don’t have to confront the coworker first; use an appropriate reporting channel.

You don’t have to get them to like you or agree with your interpretation. The goal is a workable professional relationship. What are they doing that’s making your work harder?

Start by getting specific about what’s making the relationship difficult. Are they interrupting you, missing deadlines, or sending messages that come across as dismissive? Focus on what they do and how it affects your work, rather than trying to figure out their motives. That makes it easier to decide what needs to change.

If it feels safe, bring it up privately at a calm moment. Name one example and make a concrete request: “When the deadline changed yesterday, I didn’t find out until after I’d sent the draft. Could you message me directly next time?” Then give them a chance to explain. Sometimes the issue is a mismatch in expectations, and a small agreement about how you’ll work together can help.

If the behavior continues, keep a factual record of what happened and how it affected the work. Bring it to your manager with a clear request, such as help clarifying responsibilities or setting expectations for communication. If you’re dealing with harassment, discrimination, or threats, you don’t have to confront the coworker first; use an appropriate reporting channel. The goal isn’t to make them like you. It’s to make the working relationship manageable and respectful.

A few small choices make a long-haul flight much more comfortable:

- **Pick your seat for how you fly.** Choose an aisle if you like to get up often, or a window if you want to lean against the wall and sleep.
- **Keep the essentials under the seat.** Pack an eye mask, earplugs or headphones, a warm layer, a charging cable, any medications you’ll need, and a snack. Download entertainment before boarding.
- **Sleep with your destination in mind.** If it’s nighttime there, try to sleep on board. If it’s daytime, stay awake when you can. After landing, get some daylight and aim for a local bedtime.
- **Move regularly.** Walk the aisle every couple of hours while awake when it’s safe, and do ankle circles or calf raises in your seat. If you have a history of blood clots or recently had surgery, ask your clinician about precautions before flying.
- **Drink water and go easy on alcohol.** Bring an empty bottle to refill after security. If you’re trying to sleep, skip caffeine in the hours before.
- **Plan for arrival.** Save your hotel address and transit directions offline, and keep a toothbrush and a change of underwear in your carry-on in case your checked bag is delayed.

Pack a small kit you can reach without opening the overhead bin: headphones or earplugs, an eye mask, a warm layer, lip balm, and any medication you’ll need. Download entertainment before you leave, and bring an empty water bottle to fill after security. If you like to get up often, pick an aisle seat; if you’re hoping to sleep, a window seat gives you something to lean against.

Once you board, set your clock to your destination’s time and use it as a rough guide for when to sleep. Drink water regularly, go easy on alcohol, and save caffeine for when you want to be awake. Get up and walk every couple of hours when it’s safe, and flex your ankles and calves while seated.

After landing, try to eat and sleep on local time. If you arrive during the day, spend some time outdoors and aim to stay awake until a reasonable local bedtime. If you’re too tired to function, take a short nap rather than sleeping through the afternoon.

A reliable way to make friends as an adult is to **see the same people regularly, then invite someone you click with to do something specific.** You don’t have to be especially outgoing; seeing each other again takes some of the pressure off each conversation.

1. **Pick one recurring thing you’d enjoy anyway.** A walking group, volunteer shift, class, game night, or lunch with coworkers can all work. Choose something that fits your schedule so you can show up most weeks.
2. **Build on the last conversation.** “How did that interview go?” or “Did you end up trying that restaurant?” is an easy way to go from recognizing someone to getting to know them.
3. **Make a small, concrete invitation.** Try: “I’m grabbing coffee after class next week. Want to join?” Or text someone you already like: “Hey, it’s been a while. Want to take a walk Saturday?”
4. **Give it time, but look for reciprocity.** One declined invitation usually doesn’t tell you much. If someone repeatedly declines without suggesting another time, put your energy elsewhere. Look for people who seem glad to see you, ask questions back, or make time to meet.

If you’re not sure where to start, think of one person you already enjoy talking to but rarely see. Sending them a specific invitation this week may be easier than starting from scratch.

The easiest way to make friends as an adult is to put yourself somewhere you’ll see the same people regularly. Pick something you’d enjoy even if you didn’t make a friend right away: a weekly class, a volunteer shift, a walking group, or a game night. Give it a few visits. It’s easier to start a conversation when you recognize someone and have something in common to talk about.

When you enjoy talking to someone, make a small, specific invitation. “I’m getting coffee after class next week. Want to join?” is easier to answer than “We should hang out sometime.” You can do the same with people you already know a little, like a coworker you enjoy chatting with or a neighbor you keep running into.

Don’t read too much into one declined invitation. Adults are busy, and a scheduling conflict isn’t necessarily a lack of interest. Over time, look for people who make an effort too: they suggest another day, ask how you’re doing, or reach out on their own. Friendship usually grows through ordinary moments repeated over time, not one perfect conversation.

Start with the job description. Pick the three things the employer seems to care about most, and prepare a concrete example that shows you can do each one. That’s usually more useful than memorizing answers to a long list of interview questions.

1. **Prepare a short introduction.** For “Tell me about yourself,” aim for about a minute: what you do now, one or two relevant experiences, and why this role is a logical next step.
2. **Build a small bank of stories.** Think of a success, a challenge, a mistake you learned from, and a time you worked through a disagreement. Use **STAR** (Situation, Task, Action, Result) to keep each answer focused. Spend most of your time on what *you* did and what changed as a result.
3. **Research the team and company.** Know what they do, who they serve, and what genuinely interests you about the role. Prepare two or three questions, such as “What would success look like in the first three months?” or “What’s the biggest challenge this person will help solve?”
4. **Practice out loud.** Ask a friend to run a mock interview or record yourself. Listen for answers that take too long to get to the point or make claims without examples. Practice the key points, not a script.
5. **Sort out logistics the day before.** Confirm the time and format, test your camera and mic or plan your route, and keep your résumé and a few notes handy.

If you only have 30 minutes, spend 10 reviewing the job description, 15 practicing two relevant stories aloud, and 5 writing questions for the interviewer.

Start by reading the job description and picking out the three things the employer seems to care about most. For each one, think of a specific example that shows what you can do. Research the company enough to explain, in your own words, why you want this role there. A detail about the team’s work will sound more genuine than a generic compliment.

Practice answering “Tell me about yourself” and “Why are you interested in this role?” out loud. For questions about past experience, briefly explain the situation, focus on what you did, and say what happened as a result. Don’t memorize a script; practice enough that you can tell the story naturally, even if the interviewer asks the question a different way.

Prepare a couple of questions you genuinely want answered, such as “What would a strong first three months look like?” or “What’s the biggest challenge the team is facing right now?” The day before, confirm the time and location or test the video link. During the interview, it’s fine to pause before answering or ask for clarification. You’re there to show what you can do and to find out whether the job is a good fit for you.

Make the first step small enough that you can do it even when you don’t feel ready.

1. **Pick one task and name the next action.** Not “work on the report,” but “open the document and write three rough bullet points.”
2. **Set a 10-minute timer.** Put your phone out of reach and give yourself permission to stop when the timer goes off. The goal is to start, not to finish.
3. **If you still avoid it, identify what’s in the way.** If the task is unclear, write down the first question you need answered. If you’re worried about doing it badly, make a deliberately rough first draft. If you’re exhausted, take a real break and decide when you’ll come back.

Before you stop, leave yourself a note with the next action. That way, tomorrow you can start without having to figure out where you left off.

Make the first step small enough that you can do it even when you don’t feel ready. Instead of “write the report,” try “open the document and write one rough sentence.” Set a timer for five minutes and give yourself permission to stop when it rings. The goal is to practice starting, not to finish everything in one sitting.

If you still keep putting it off, ask what makes the task hard to start. If it’s unclear, decide what “done” looks like. If you’re worried about doing it badly, make a rough first pass that no one else has to see. If you keep reaching for your phone, put it in another room before you sit down. Addressing the specific obstacle usually helps more than telling yourself to try harder.

Pick one thing you’ve been avoiding and decide exactly when you’ll take that first step: “After lunch, I’ll sit at my desk and work on it for five minutes.” If you miss that window, pick another one instead of writing off the day. Getting back to the task is a skill you can practice, too.

If you’re feeling stressed right now, start small: take a few slow, comfortable breaths, unclench your jaw and shoulders, and ask yourself, “What’s one thing I can do next?” You don’t have to solve everything at once.

A few other things to try:

- **Move a little.** A short walk, some gentle stretching, or dancing to one song can help you reset.
- **Get it out of your head.** Write down what’s weighing on you. Pick one thing to act on and one thing you can postpone, delegate, or drop.
- **Talk to someone you trust.** Tell them whether you’d like advice, practical help, or just someone to listen.
- **Make room for recovery.** Take short breaks before you’re exhausted, keep a regular sleep schedule where possible, and notice whether caffeine makes you feel more on edge.
- **Address the source when you can.** If the same demand keeps wearing you down, asking for help, setting a boundary, or renegotiating a deadline may do more than another relaxation exercise.

Pick one that feels doable today. If stress keeps interfering with sleep, work, or relationships, a healthcare professional or therapist can help you figure out what’s driving it and what support might help.

When stress spikes, try slowing your breathing for a minute or two, letting each exhale be a little longer than the inhale. A short walk, a stretch, or a few minutes away from your screen can also help you settle enough to decide what to do next.

If you’re overwhelmed by everything you have to do, write it down and pick one small step you can take now. It can help to ask what can wait, what you can say no to, and what someone else could help with. Talking to a friend can make things feel less isolating, even if they don’t have a solution.

Over time, regular sleep, meals, and movement can make stress easier to manage. Start with one change that fits your day rather than turning stress relief into another chore. If stress is sticking around or interfering with sleep, work, or relationships, consider talking with a healthcare professional or counselor.

Start with walking, then mix in short, easy jogs. Your first goal is to finish feeling like you could do a little more—not to run a mile or hit a certain pace.

1. **Find a comfortable starting point.** Walk for 5–15 minutes, three days a week. If five minutes feels like enough, start there. Build up until a 20-minute walk feels comfortable.
2. **Try your first run-walk session.** Walk for 5 minutes to warm up. Then jog gently for 20–30 seconds and walk for 90 seconds. Repeat 5 times, then finish with a few minutes of easy walking. Jog slowly enough that you can still speak in full sentences.
3. **Repeat before you add more.** Leave a rest day between run-walk sessions. Once the same workout feels comfortable for several outings, add one repeat *or* make the jogs a little longer. There’s no need to do both at once.

Comfortable shoes and a flat route are enough to get started. Mild muscle soreness can happen, but don’t push through sharp or worsening pain. Stop and seek urgent medical help if you develop chest pain, feel faint, or have severe shortness of breath. If you have a heart or lung condition or already experience symptoms with light activity, ask a clinician before adding jogging.

Start with a 10- to 15-minute walk at a comfortable pace, two or three times a week. If that feels like too much, start with five minutes. For the first week or two, just get used to moving regularly. You don’t need to run on day one.

Once you can walk briskly for 20 minutes and feel fine the next day, try adding short jogs. Walk for five minutes to warm up, then jog gently for 20 to 30 seconds and walk for two minutes. Repeat that a few times and finish with an easy walk. Keep the jog slow enough that you can still speak in full sentences, and take a day off between runs.

Repeat the same routine until it feels comfortable, then make the jogs a little longer or add one more interval. There’s no rush to run without walking. Some mild muscle soreness is normal, but stop if you get sharp pain, chest pain, feel faint, or have unusual trouble breathing. If you have a heart or lung condition or symptoms when you walk, check with a healthcare professional before adding jogging.

Ask in writing—by email, text, or your landlord’s maintenance portal—so you have a record. Say what’s broken, when it started, and how it’s affecting you. Include a photo if it helps, and ask when someone can come by.

**Template:**

> Hi [Landlord’s name], I’m writing to request a repair in [unit/address]. The [item] has been [describe the problem] since [date]. Could you let me know when someone can come by to fix it? I’m available [times], or we can arrange another time. Thanks, [Your name]

For an urgent issue like an active leak, call the emergency maintenance number first, then follow up in writing. If a routine request goes unanswered, reply to your original message so the date and details stay in one place.

Ask in writing so you both have a record. Say what needs fixing, when you noticed it, and how it’s affecting you. If a photo would help show the problem, attach one. Ask when someone can come by rather than leaving the timing open-ended.

Hi [Landlord’s name], I’m writing about [problem] in my unit at [address or unit number]. I first noticed it on [date], and it’s [briefly explain the impact]. Could you please arrange a repair and let me know when someone can come by? I’m available [times], but I can coordinate another time if needed. Thanks, [Your name].

If the problem is urgent, say why in the first sentence and call the emergency maintenance number if your building has one. If it’s not urgent and you don’t hear back after a few days, reply to your original message and ask for an update.

The easiest way to save on a wedding is to **set your spending limit and guest list before you book a venue**. A smaller guest list cuts food, drinks, rentals, and sometimes the venue cost itself.

1. **Set an all-in budget.** Count only money you and any contributors have committed. Set aside about 10% for surprises, and track deposits and final payment dates in a simple spreadsheet.
2. **Pick two or three priorities.** If what matters most is good food and photos with your family, spend there. Keep invitations, flowers, and favors simple—or skip them.
3. **Compare venues by total cost, not rental fee.** Ask for a written quote that includes catering minimums, tables and chairs, staffing, cleanup, taxes, and service charges. A restaurant with a private room may cost less than a bare hall once you add rentals.
4. **Get creative with timing and format.** Price a brunch, Sunday lunch, or off-season date. A courthouse ceremony followed by a restaurant meal can feel special without requiring a full day of vendors.
5. **Cut whole expenses before trying to DIY them.** Digital invitations, no favors, and a shorter photography package can save more time and money than making dozens of decorations. If you DIY, choose things you can finish well before the wedding.

For example, if your cap is **$6,000**, reserve **$600** for surprises. If the ceremony, attire, photography, and other fixed costs come to **$1,800**, you have **$3,600** for the reception. For **40 guests**, that’s **$90 per guest all-in** for the space, food, drinks, and fees—a useful number to bring when asking for quotes.

If you share your approximate budget, guest count, and location, I can help you sketch a realistic budget and decide what to book first.

Start with what you can comfortably afford, not what a wedding is “supposed” to cost. If family is contributing, confirm how much before you book anything. Decide together what matters most to you, whether that’s a great meal, photos you’ll keep for years, or having everyone you love in the room. Set aside a little of your budget for surprises so a last-minute expense doesn’t throw everything off.

A good CV makes it easy for a hiring manager to see **what you can do, where you’ve done it, and why it matters for this role**. Start with the job description, then put your strongest relevant evidence near the top.

### Use a simple structure

- **Contact details:** Name, email, phone number, city or region, and a LinkedIn or portfolio link if it adds value.
- **Profile (optional):** Two or three lines about your experience and what you bring to the role. Skip it if it would just say you’re “hardworking and motivated.”
- **Experience:** List your most recent role first. Include your title, employer, dates, and a few bullets showing what you accomplished.
- **Education and skills:** Include relevant qualifications, tools, languages, or certifications. If you’re early in your career, relevant coursework, projects, or volunteering can provide evidence just as well as paid work.

### Write bullets that show results

Instead of listing duties, explain what you did and what changed. For example:

> **Vague:** Responsible for weekly sales reports.  
> **Stronger:** Automated weekly sales reports in Excel, cutting preparation time from three hours to 45 minutes.

Use numbers when you can verify them. If you don’t have metrics, describe the scope or outcome: who used your work, what problem it solved, or what you delivered.

### Tailor it before you send it

Pick the three or four most important requirements in the job ad. For each one you meet, check that your CV gives a clear example. Use the employer’s terminology where it accurately describes your experience, and trim details that distract from your strongest evidence.

Keep the layout easy to scan: clear headings, consistent dates, and readable type. ## A simple sourdough loaf

You’ll need an **active sourdough starter**. Use it when it’s bubbly and has roughly doubled after feeding. If you don’t have one yet, you can get some from a friend or bakery, or grow your own from flour and water.

### Ingredients
- 500 g bread flour
- 350 g water
- 100 g active starter
- 10 g fine salt

### Steps
1. **Mix.** Stir the starter into the water, then add the flour and salt. Mix until no dry flour remains. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.
2. **Fold.** With a damp hand, pull one edge of the dough up and fold it over the center. Turn the bowl and repeat on all four sides. Do three sets of folds, about 30 minutes apart.
3. **Let it rise.** Keep the dough covered at room temperature until it looks puffy, has bubbles along the sides, and has grown by about half. In a warm kitchen, this often takes 4–6 hours **from mixing**, including the time spent folding. A cooler kitchen can take longer.
4. **Shape and chill.** Turn the dough onto a lightly floured counter and shape it into a tight round. Place it seam-side up in a bowl lined with a well-floured kitchen towel. Cover and refrigerate for 8–16 hours.
5. **Bake.** Preheat a Dutch oven at **450°F (230°C)** for 30 minutes. Turn the cold dough onto baking parchment, slash the top with a sharp blade, and lower it into the pot. Bake **25 minutes covered**, then **20–25 minutes uncovered**, until deeply golden brown.
6. **Cool.** Let the loaf cool on a rack for at least an hour before slicing so the crumb has time to set.

**The best beginner tip:** Watch the dough, not the clock. If it still looks dense after the suggested rise time, give it longer before shaping.

Over the next 2 hours, stretch and fold the dough every 30 minutes: lift one edge, fold it over the center, and repeat on all four sides. Then leave it covered until it looks puffy, has bubbles along the edges, and has grown by about half. That might take 4 to 7 hours total from when you mixed the dough, including the folds. Go by how the dough looks rather than by the clock.

Turn the cold dough out onto parchment, make a shallow slash across the top with a sharp blade, and carefully lower it into the hot pot. Bake covered for 25 minutes, then uncovered for another 20 to 25 minutes, until the crust is deep golden brown. Let it cool on a rack for at least an hour before slicing so the inside has time to set.

For example, if a basket of groceries cost $100 last year and the same items cost $105 this year, the price of that basket rose by 5%. Economists measure inflation by tracking a much wider mix of things people buy, such as food, rent, and gas. Not every price has to rise for there to be inflation.

**Rule of thumb:** If you qualify for the traditional IRA deduction and expect a lower tax rate in retirement, a traditional IRA may be the better fit. A Roth IRA may make more sense if you expect your tax rate to be higher in retirement than it is now. A traditional IRA may make more sense if you can take the deduction today and expect a lower tax rate when you withdraw the money.

Compound interest is **interest earned on both your original money and the interest you’ve already earned**. That means your balance can grow by a little more each year, even if the interest rate stays the same.

Suppose you deposit **$1,000** at **5% interest, compounded annually**, and leave it untouched:

| Year | Interest earned that year | End-of-year balance |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | $50.00 | $1,050.00 |
| 2 | $52.50 | $1,102.50 |
| 3 | $55.13 | $1,157.63 |

In year 2, you earn 5% of **$1,050**, not just 5% of the original $1,000. That extra $2.50 is interest on the interest from year 1. With **simple interest**, by contrast, you’d earn $50 each year.

The same effect can work against you on debt: if unpaid interest is added to what you owe, future interest can be charged on that larger balance.

Compound interest means you earn interest on both the money you started with and the interest you’ve already earned. When interest is added to your balance, the next round of interest is calculated on that larger amount.

For example, if you put $1,000 in an account that earns 5% interest each year, you’ll earn $50 in the first year. If you leave that money in the account, you’ll start the second year with $1,050. This time, 5% earns you $52.50, bringing your balance to $1,102.50.

The longer you leave the money alone, the more those extra earnings can add up. Compounding can also work against you when you borrow: if unpaid interest is added to what you owe, you can end up paying interest on that interest too.

# What a Year of Journaling Taught Me

I started journaling because I wanted to remember more of my life. A year later, I’m surprised by what I’m glad I wrote down. It’s not the big decisions I spent pages agonizing over. It’s the evening a friend stayed on the phone while I folded laundry, or the first morning it was warm enough to drink my coffee outside.

Reading back also showed me how often I mistook a bad day for a verdict. One Tuesday, I wrote that I was tired of everything. On Wednesday, my entire entry was about a sandwich I’d made with the good bread. The sandwich didn’t solve anything, but I’m glad it made the record.

I missed plenty of days. At first, I’d open the notebook after a week away and feel obliged to explain the gap. Eventually, I learned to skip the apology and start with whatever had happened that morning.

I still don’t write every day. But I notice more while I’m living it. Sometimes, halfway through a perfectly ordinary afternoon, I think: I want to remember this.

When I started journaling, I thought I’d end up with a record of the big things that happened that year. Instead, I wrote a lot about being tired, putting off phone calls, and feeling better after going for a walk. The big things are in there too, but the small stuff taught me more about how I actually spend my days.

Reading old entries, I noticed how often I’d written “for no reason” after describing a bad mood. Sometimes the reason was right there on the page: I’d skipped lunch, said yes to something I didn’t want to do, or spent all afternoon rehearsing a conversation that took five minutes. I still do those things. I just catch myself a little sooner now.

I also got less precious about what counted as journaling. Some nights I wrote three pages. Other nights I wrote one sentence and went to bed. A year later, I’m glad I kept both kinds of entries. It turns out a sentence like “We ate peaches over the sink” can bring back a whole day I would’ve sworn I’d forgotten.

At 35, I took my first coding class at the kitchen table after work. I’d spent more than a decade in operations, where people came to me when a shipment went missing or a spreadsheet stopped making sense. Now I was spending an entire evening trying to figure out why a button wouldn’t work. The hardest part wasn’t finding the time to learn. It was going from being someone people asked for help to someone who needed it constantly.

My first project was a small tool that flagged duplicate orders in a spreadsheet. I built it because checking those orders by hand was a Friday afternoon chore I hated. The first version flagged two legitimate orders from the same customer, which was exactly the kind of mistake I knew to look for from my old job. Fixing it made me realize I wasn’t starting from scratch. I was learning a new way to solve problems I already understood.

The job search took longer than I’d hoped. In one interview, I blanked on a question about a piece of code I’d written myself. In another, I spent most of the conversation talking about how I’d decide whether a feature was ready for the people who actually had to use it. That was the interview that got me my first tech job. The starting salary was lower than what I’d been making, and I went over the numbers more than once before I said yes.

A few months into the job, a colleague showed me how to fix a bug I’d been staring at all morning. Later that week, she asked me to help her untangle a confusing request from another department. We drew out the process on a whiteboard, and I spotted a handoff nobody had accounted for. It felt good to be useful in a way I recognized. It also felt good, finally, not to mind being the person who asked for help.

## What I Kept

I thought minimalism would make my apartment look better. Mostly, it made getting out the door easier.

I started with the pile by the front door: shoes I never wore, unopened mail, a tote bag full of smaller tote bags. Once I cleared it, I put a little dish there for my keys. It’s been months since I’ve had to check yesterday’s pants five minutes before leaving.

I still have too many mugs. One has a chipped handle, and another is so big the coffee goes cold before I finish it. I like them both. The longer I do this, the less interested I am in owning the fewest things possible. I’d rather be able to find my keys, make a cup of coffee, and get on with my morning.

I thought minimalism would start with a dramatic weekend of clearing things out. Instead, it started with my kitchen drawer. I pulled out three spatulas, realized I always reached for the same one, and put the other two in a donation bag. The next morning, I opened the drawer and found what I wanted without having to dig. That small thing felt better than I expected.

I’ve gotten better at noticing what I actually use, but I still keep things that don’t earn their space in any practical way. There’s a chipped mug I could easily replace. It’s also the mug I reach for on slow Saturday mornings, so it stays.

The biggest change is that I pause before bringing something home. Sometimes I still buy it. Other times I realize I liked it perfectly well on the shelf and don’t need to find a place for it in my life.

# How to Stay Motivated While Learning to Code

Learning to code can feel slow because progress doesn’t always look like a finished project. Sometimes it looks like finally understanding an error message that stumped you yesterday. That counts.

**Build something you want to use.** A quiz for your friends or a script that renames your photos can make practice feel worthwhile. Start with the smallest version that works. A quiz with three questions teaches you more than an ambitious app you never start.

**Give each session one clear goal.** Instead of “learn JavaScript,” try “make this button change the text.” A goal you can finish in 20 minutes makes it easier to sit down and gives you a clear win when you’re done.

**Keep a record of what clicked.** Write down one thing you learned or one bug you fixed. When you feel stuck, look back at your notes. Problems that once took an hour may now take five minutes, and it’s easy to miss that kind of progress.

You don’t have to feel motivated every time you practice. Before you stop, leave yourself a specific next step. “Check why the score resets” is a much easier place to pick up than “keep learning to code.”

Learning to code is easier to stick with when you have a reason to open your editor. Pick a small project you’d actually use, like a page that tracks the books you’ve read. Start with the simplest version: show one book on the page. Adding a second book tomorrow is a better goal than trying to build an entire app tonight.

On days when you’re stuck, make the task smaller. Instead of “fix this bug,” try “figure out why this button does nothing.” Even if you don’t solve it, write down what you ruled out and what you’ll try next. That note makes it easier to come back, and it reminds you that debugging counts as progress.

Don’t let a missed day turn into a reason to quit. A routine you can return to matters more than a perfect streak. Every so often, revisit something you built a few weeks ago. A line of code you once had to look up might now make sense at a glance. That’s progress you can see.

# I Switched Careers Into Tech at 35. The Hardest Part Was Being New Again.

On my first morning as a junior developer, I spent forty minutes trying to get the company’s app to run on my laptop. Then I spent another twenty deciding whether I’d been stuck long enough to ask for help.

In my old job in operations, people came to me when something broke. I knew which spreadsheet was lying, which supplier would pick up before eight, and which “quick question” meant I should cancel lunch. Now I was composing a message that said, essentially, *I followed the instructions and nothing happened.* I rewrote it three times.

My teammate replied in two minutes. The instructions were out of date.

## I didn’t quit my job and spend six months finding myself

I had rent. I had a modest savings account that I wanted to keep modestly intact. So I started with a free programming course after work and gave myself permission to stop if I hated it.

Some nights, I did hate it. I once lost an entire Thursday to a missing bracket. But I liked the feeling of making something I could actually use. One of my first projects was a script that cleaned up a weekly report at work. It saved me about fifteen minutes, which was less time than I’d spent explaining to my partner why it wasn’t working. The next week, though, I got those fifteen minutes back. And the week after that.

That little script told me more about whether I’d enjoy the work than any number of videos about becoming a developer. I liked taking an annoying task apart, figuring out which bits needed to happen in what order, and making the whole thing a little less annoying.

## My old career wasn’t a detour

At first, I wrote my résumé as if I’d sprung into existence the day I learned JavaScript. My projects went at the top; nearly a decade of work got squeezed into a few lines at the bottom. I thought hiring managers wanted proof that I was technical, so I hid most of the evidence that I knew how to work.

In the interview that led to my first offer, the hiring manager asked how I handled vague requests. I told her about a manager who’d asked for a “better inventory report.” After watching him use the old one, I realized he didn’t need more data. He needed to know, before he placed an order on Fridays, which items were about to run out.

We spent more time talking about that report than we did about my portfolio. Months later, on the job, I caught myself doing the same thing: asking a colleague to show me what she did on a Tuesday morning instead of asking her to describe the feature she wanted. I was still slow at reading unfamiliar code. I was already good at that conversation.

## Being a beginner got less embarrassing

There were real trade-offs. I took a pay cut. I had less say over my work. It was strange to be the person who needed a walkthrough after years of being the person who gave one. What helped wasn’t becoming fearless about asking questions. It was getting better at asking them: *Here’s what I expected. Here’s what happened. Here’s what I’ve tried.*

A few months in, another new developer messaged me because she couldn’t get the app to run. I recognized the error. I sent her the fix, then opened the setup guide and corrected the instructions I’d stumbled over on my first day.

It wasn’t a big technical achievement. But I remember how pleased I was to make that edit. I’d spent so much time wondering when I’d stop being the new person that I hadn’t noticed I’d already become someone who could make the next person’s first morning easier.
